# Sukhi Play: the manual and the blog, in full

> A free locked-down browser for small children, for macOS, Windows and Linux,
> made by Mandeep Singh for his own son. This file holds every page of the
> documentation and every blog post. The brief is at https://sukhiplay.com/llms.txt.

## Installing

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/installing/

> Every way to install Sukhi Play on macOS, Windows and Linux, and what to expect the first time it opens.

On Ubuntu and any other distribution with snap, this is the easiest way and it
updates itself:

```bash
sudo snap install sukhi-play
```

One thing to know about the snap: it runs under strict confinement, which is
what keeps its permissions restricted, and a confined snap is not allowed to
change desktop settings. So it does not borrow Alt+Tab and the Super key the
way the `.deb` and `.AppImage` do. Everything else is identical. If that layer
matters to you, use one of those instead.

On macOS, the two links below always point at the newest release. There is a
[dedicated macOS page](/macos/) covering which one to pick and the
first-launch warning.

| Platform | File |
| --- | --- |
| macOS (Apple Silicon) | **[Sukhi-Play-macOS-AppleSilicon.dmg](https://github.com/meSingh/sukhi-play/releases/latest/download/Sukhi-Play-macOS-AppleSilicon.dmg)** |
| macOS (Intel) | **[Sukhi-Play-macOS-Intel.dmg](https://github.com/meSingh/sukhi-play/releases/latest/download/Sukhi-Play-macOS-Intel.dmg)** |
| Windows 10 / 11 | **[Sukhi-Play-Windows-Setup.exe](https://github.com/meSingh/sukhi-play/releases/latest/download/Sukhi-Play-Windows-Setup.exe)**, or [portable](https://github.com/meSingh/sukhi-play/releases/latest/download/Sukhi-Play-Windows-Portable.exe) |
| Ubuntu / Debian | `.deb` |
| Other Linux | `.AppImage`, `chmod +x` then run |

Everything else is on the
**[latest release](https://github.com/meSingh/sukhi-play/releases/latest)**
page.

> **These builds are signed, but not notarised.** Notarising needs a paid
> Apple Developer account and an EV certificate is needed for Windows, both
> annual, and this is a free project. `SHA256SUMS.txt` is attached to every
> release if you want to check what you downloaded.
>
> **macOS** blocks the first launch with *"Apple could not verify Sukhi Play is
> free of malware"*. Control-clicking the app and choosing *Open* used to get
> past this, but macOS 15 removed that. The route is **System Settings** →
> **Privacy & Security** → **Open Anyway**, under *Security* at the bottom.
> Once per install. [Full walkthrough, with the one-line
> alternative](/macos/).
>
> **Windows** SmartScreen shows *"Windows protected your PC"*. Click **More
> info**, then **Run anyway** — the button only appears after More info.
> [Full walkthrough, including how to check the hash](/windows/).

Or run it from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/meSingh/sukhi-play.git
cd sukhi-play
npm install
npm start
```

## The first run

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/first-run/

> What the walkthrough asks you, and what happens once it is done.

The first time you open Sukhi Play it asks **who is using the computer right
now**: a grown-up setting it up, or someone just looking. Choose *I'm a
grown-up* and it walks you through four short steps:

1. **What this is.** What your child will and will not be able to reach.
2. **Choose what they can open.** Pick one or two sites from the suggestions.
3. **How you get back out.** It explains the ✕ and the three-second hold, and
   lets you practise the hold once so you know the feel of it.
4. **Hand it over.**

That is the whole setup. Afterwards the walkthrough never appears again, and the
tile screen is what opens.

If the tile screen is ever empty it says so plainly and offers a button that
takes you to the grown-up screen, with no hunting through files.

## Adding and removing sites

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/adding-sites/

> Take one from the catalogue, or paste any address and let the app work out what it needs.

**Sukhi Play does not pick websites for you.** What it ships enabled is three
of the apps that live inside the download -- [Sukhi Colouring](/docs/sukhi-colouring/),
a keyboard playground and first games -- because those are files on your own
disk with no network behind them and nobody's terms to accept. A fourth,
[Jazz's Studio](/docs/jazz-studio/), is for older children and waits in the
catalogue until you add it. Every website is yours to
add, and you never need to work out hostnames yourself.

Open the grown-up screen (**Grown-ups**, hold 3 seconds). Four tabs: play time,
installed apps, the catalogue, and settings.

### The catalogue, in one tap

Sites that are known to work, grouped by category and labelled **no ads**,
**ads filtered** or **ads showing**. Tap one and it arrives on the tile screen
with the hosts it needs already filled in.

The list is not reproduced here: it would drift the moment it changed, and it
has. It lives at **[sukhiplay.com/catalogue](https://sukhiplay.com/catalogue/)**
and in [config/suggestions.json](https://github.com/meSingh/sukhi-play/blob/main/config/suggestions.json), which is the one file
both the app and the site are built from.

Nothing in it is endorsed by this project, and none of those sites is connected
to it. Read [DISCLAIMER.md](https://github.com/meSingh/sukhi-play/blob/main/DISCLAIMER.md).

### Create a custom app: type an address and it works out the rest

Type `pbskids.org`. The app opens it once, watches every request it makes, and
tells you:

```
Found 1 host. 2 looked like advertising or tracking and will be blocked.
  pbskids.org
```

Give the tile a name, press **Save**, and it writes the allowlist for you. This
is the same machinery as `npm run check`, driven from the interface. Pick one of
the sixteen shapes and a colour for the tile: a site's own favicon is its
trademark, and this project has no licence to put one on a tile or in a
release.

### Your apps: turn things on and off

Each app is a card shaped like the tile your child sees. The switch in its
corner decides whether it appears on their screen, and tapping the card opens
everything else: name, picture, colour, address, allowed hosts and ad filtering,
with Delete at the bottom.

<div align="center">
<picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="/img/screenshots/02-parent-portal-800.webp 800w, /img/screenshots/02-parent-portal-1240.webp 1240w, /img/screenshots/02-parent-portal-1400.webp 1400w" sizes="(min-width: 800px) 760px, 94vw">
<img src="/screenshots/02-parent-portal.png" width="760" height="486" loading="lazy" alt="The grown-up screen: tabs for play time, installed apps, the catalogue and settings, with a card and an on/off switch for each app"></picture>
</div>

### Leaving a site as its operator intended

Some sites say plainly in their terms that you may not interfere with their
advertising. `blockAds: false` is available on any site you add, for exactly
that case. Containment still applies in full: your child cannot leave the site,
open a popup, or reach anything else.

**youtube.com is deliberately not in the catalogue.** Recommendations, comments
and autoplay make it unsuitable for a small child.

## Play time

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/play-time/

> Set how long a session lasts, and what happens when it runs out.

Set a session length on the **Play time** tab of the grown-up screen: any
number of minutes up to four hours, or no limit at all. It is a standing rule,
not a decision you make each time -- the clock starts again every time Sukhi
Play opens.

Your child sees no countdown while they play. It appears only in the last
thirty seconds, or the last ten on a session of five minutes or less, so there
is nothing to watch or bargain with. When the time is up they get a stop
screen and nothing else opens.

## Giving more time

From the stop screen your child can ask, and only a grown-up can answer: the
same hold or sum as anywhere else, and then a choice of fifteen minutes, an
hour, or the rest of the day.

Whatever you grant applies to **that session only**. Your usual limit does not
move, so giving an hour today does not quietly make every day an hour. The
next time the app opens it starts from your rule again.

If you would rather not grant anything, the stop screen also has a way out for
a grown-up to close Sukhi Play. The clock is counted in the
main process, never in the page: a site your child is on shares that page's
process, and a clock a game could stop is not a clock. The gate and the portal
pause it, so setting up a new site does not spend your child's afternoon.

It is a session, not a day. Nothing is stored between runs, because a stored
daily total invites the question "what counts as a day", and answering it
wrongly means telling a two-year-old their time is gone at breakfast.

## The grown-up gate

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/the-gate/

> The hold, the sum, and everything that sits behind them.

Press ✕, or **Ctrl+Shift+X** (**Cmd+Shift+X** on a Mac).

**Grown-ups** opens the portal. **Close** quits. Either way you hold a button
for 3 seconds first, and the gate says which one you asked for.

The hold is **timed in the main process**, not the page. The animation is only
for you to look at, and letting go early gets you nothing.

## The sum, instead of the hold

If your child ever works the hold out, switch **Getting in here** on the
Settings tab from *Hold* to *Sum*. You are then asked a small addition instead,
and holding the button stops opening anything at all -- it is one way in or the
other, never both.

Wrong answers get a fresh sum, and three of them in a row lock the gate for ten
seconds.

## The grown-up screen

Four tabs: **Play time**, **Installed apps**, **Catalogue** and **Settings**.
Quitting is in the corner rather than buried in a menu. Besides adding and
editing apps:

- **Check for updates** asks GitHub whether a newer release exists and links to
  it. It reports only. Nothing is downloaded or installed, because a kiosk that
  can rewrite itself is a worse problem than one that is out of date.
- **Reset Sukhi Play to factory settings** wipes every app and setting and
  restarts into the walkthrough. It asks twice and cannot be undone.

> A `.deb` or `.dmg` you installed by hand is not tracked by your system's app
> store, so it will never offer you an update. That is how manual packages
> work rather than a fault in this app. Use **Check for updates** and download
> the new one.

A PIN is also available, for anyone who would rather type one. Unlike the sum,
it comes *after* the hold rather than instead of it:

```json
{ "gateMode": "pin", "pin": "4821" }
```

### Settings

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gateMode` | `"hold"` | `"hold"`, `"sum"` to answer an addition instead, or `"pin"` to also require a PIN after the hold |
| `holdSeconds` | `3` | Seconds the exit button must be held (1–15) |
| `kiosk` | `true` | Cover the whole screen, no window chrome |
| `alwaysOnTop` | `true` | Keep the window above everything else |
| `refocusOnBlur` | `true` | Pull the window back if the child clicks away |
| `showBlockCounter` | `true` | Show "N ads blocked" in the bar |
| `onboarded` | `false` | Set to `false` to see the first-run walkthrough again |
| `borrowDesktopShortcuts` | `true` | Linux/GNOME only. Switch the desktop's Alt+Tab and Super key off while the app runs, then restore them |

`refocusOnBlur` switches itself off if it ever starts fighting another window,
so it can never make the machine unusable.

## What your child sees

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/what-child-sees/

> The tile screen, and what is deliberately not on it.

1. **A loading screen.**
2. **The picker.** Big square tiles, one per site, each a bold colour and a
   simple shape. No reading needed.
3. **The site**, with a thin bar on top: a large blue **Back** button and a small
   grey **✕** in the corner.

The tile screen scrolls once there are more games than fit on the screen, so
nothing ends up stranded above or below where a small child cannot reach it.

There is no fullscreen button. The app already covers the screen, and there is
nothing a child can press to shrink it.

## Sukhi Colouring

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/sukhi-colouring/

> The colouring book built into Sukhi Play: what it does, where drawings are kept, and how to use it on any device.

Sukhi Colouring is the colouring book that comes with Sukhi Play. It is the
first app in the [playground](/playground/): little apps we make ourselves for
Sukhi Play, rather than websites you allow. More are on the way.

## Where to find it

- **In Sukhi Play** it is the **Colouring** tile, switched on from the start.
  It is part of the download, so it works with no internet at all.
- **On any other device** open
  [sukhiplay.com/playground/colouring](/playground/colouring/) in a browser.
  Nothing to install and nothing to sign up for.

## What your child can do

- **Pick a picture** with the pictures button: forty to choose from, or leave
  it and draw on a blank page.
- **Draw** with the pencil, the crayon or the rainbow, in three widths.
- **Tap to fill** a shape inside the picture. Tapping the paper around it
  colours the whole page instead.
- **Mirror drawing**, the butterfly, copies everything onto the other side.
- **Rub out** with the eraser under the colours.
- **Back** and **Forward** undo and redo. **Start again** clears the page, and
  asks first.

## Saving their pictures

Press **Keep it** and the picture goes into **My pictures**. Open one from there
and it comes back exactly as it was left, ready to carry on colouring. The
download button under each saves a copy as an image file, and the bin removes
it, after asking.

Pictures are kept **on that device only**. Nothing is uploaded, and there is no
account for them to be tied to. My pictures holds the sixty most recent; the
oldest make way for new ones. Clearing the browser's data for the site, or
using a private window, clears them too.

## Settings

The cog holds the language, English or 한국어, and the sound on or off. It sits
at the end of the tools, out of the way of the ones a child uses most.

## On a phone or tablet

It works the same on a small screen, with the tools along the top and the
colours along the bottom.

To keep it on the home screen, press **Add to home screen** in the app: the
phone with an arrow in it, next to the cog. It shows the steps for the device
you are on, and in Chrome or Edge it has an **Install** button that does it in
one tap. The steps, in case you would rather do it yourself:

- **iPhone and iPad:** open it in Safari, tap **Share**, then
  **Add to Home Screen**.
- **Android:** open it in Chrome, open the menu, then **Add to Home screen**.
- **A computer:** in Chrome or Edge, click the install icon at the end of the
  address bar.

It then opens full screen like any other app, and keeps working without
internet once it has been opened once.

## Jazz's Studio

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/jazz-studio/

> The stationery studio built into Sukhi Play for older children: what it makes, how printing works, and where their things are kept.

Jazz's Studio is the second app in the [playground](/playground/), and the
first for older children, about seven and up. It was made for Jazz, who is
ten, and your child can use all of it, with their own name on everything and,
if you like, their own character in place of Jazz's.

## Where to find it

- **In Sukhi Play** it comes in the download but is **not switched on**, so a
  younger child's screen stays as it was. Open the grown-up screen, go to the
  catalogue, and add **Studio**. It works with no internet at all.
- **On any other device** open
  [sukhiplay.com/playground/studio](/playground/studio/) in a browser. Nothing
  to install and nothing to sign up for.

## What your child can do

- **Stationery:** in five groups: stickers (of their characters, or in their
  pattern), a diary cover and pages, name labels and gift tags, a week planner
  and to-do lists, and bookmarks and door signs. Each sheet keeps its own
  colours, lettering and pattern, and a sheet with several people on it has
  each one's own name, changed right there.
- **Make from a box:** pick a pencil pot, desk tidy, notebook cover or treasure
  box, measure the tube or box, and print a wrap that fits it, with the steps.
- **My brand:** a brand for each person, in four styles (badge, stamp, ribbon
  and tag), business cards, and logo stickers cut out round the logo. A diary
  with someone on it carries their brand.
- **Play:** a poster of their name, secret messages in a real code with a key
  for a friend, a story page built from who, what happens and where, a doodle
  pad, and invite cards with a code a friend's phone opens the studio from.
- **My makes:** their prints, kept to print again, and a shelf of the things
  they made.
- **Make it yours:** their character and name, and the look of the studio: its
  colours, lettering and background. Start again is a tab of its own, and asks
  first.

## Printing

Every sheet is drawn on A4 to the millimetre, and prints on one page. In a
browser, print wraps for **Make from a box** at **actual size**, not "fit to
page", so they fit the thing they were measured for; each wrap has a line that
should measure exactly 5 cm, so a ruler can check.

On an **iPad**, Safari prints the page's address and the date at the top and
bottom and always prints a little smaller than actual size, so the sheet is
fitted into what is left. That is fine for stickers and planners; for a wrap,
measure the 5 cm line.

**Inside Sukhi Play there is no print window.** A print window can save to a
file or open another program, both ways out of the locked screen, so Sukhi
Play sends the page straight to the computer's **default printer** instead,
and the studio tells your child when it has gone, or to ask a grown-up if the
printer did not answer. Two presses a few seconds apart print once.

Only apps Sukhi Play made itself can print. A website that tries to print is
refused.

## The first time, and their characters

The first time the studio opens it asks two things, either of which can be
skipped: their **name**, so it says hello to them, and their **character**:
Jazz, her brother Sukhi, or one of their own. **Start again** asks again.

In **Make it yours**, the list at the top is every character, each switched on
or off. **Add a character** is someone new: it takes a picture of a character
on one plain colour, cuts the background out on the device, finds the face so
stickers and labels frame it, and then asks **who this is**, their name or
"It's me". Each person then has **Add a picture** for more of them, and their
name goes with them onto their stickers, labels and tags. Pictures can be
nudged if the face is framed badly, or removed.

The studio has a **For grown-ups** guide that walks through making one from a
photo with Google Gemini, with the prompts that made Jazz's. When you use
Gemini the photo goes to Google; nothing you add to the studio leaves the
device.

Inside Sukhi Play no page may open a file browser, so there a grown-up copies
the picture and presses **Ctrl+V** (**Cmd+V** on a Mac) in Make it yours.

## Prints to use again

After something is printed, the studio asks whether to keep it in **My makes**
and what to call it; there is also a **Keep in My makes** button beside Print.
It keeps the print's settings, not a picture of it: which sheet, the words,
which character, and its colours, lettering and pattern. **Open** puts the
tool back exactly as it was, to print again or change something first. A kept
print keeps its colours even if the studio's change later.

## Photos and their things

**My makes** also keeps each thing they made: its name, a note, and a photo.
In a browser a photo can be taken or chosen. Inside Sukhi Play, which never
opens a file browser, a grown-up copies a photo and presses **Ctrl+V**
(**Cmd+V** on a Mac) on My makes, or drags one onto the photo box. Doodles
from the doodle pad keep their picture everywhere.

Everything is kept **on that device only**: nothing is uploaded, and there is
no account. Clearing the browser's data for the site, or using a private
window, clears it too.

## On a phone or tablet

To keep it on the home screen:

- **iPhone and iPad:** open it in Safari, tap **Share**, then
  **Add to Home Screen**.
- **Android:** open it in Chrome, open the menu, then **Add to Home screen**.
- **A computer:** in Chrome or Edge, click the install icon at the end of the
  address bar.

It then opens full screen like any other app, and keeps working without
internet once it has been opened once.

## How the lockdown works

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/lockdown/

> Every layer between your child and the rest of the computer, and what each one actually does.

Six independent layers, so no single mistake opens a hole.

**1. An allowlist per site.** Each entry lists the only hosts allowed to load
*anything at all*. Every other request is cancelled: image, script, frame, websocket. This layer does most of the work: it blocks ad networks nobody has
heard of yet, because they are not on the list.

**2. An ad and tracker blocklist.** ~110 known ad, tracker and popunder domains
plus URL patterns, checked *even on allowed hosts*. This catches ad code served
from a site's own CDN, which an allowlist alone cannot see.

**3. No new windows.** Every popup, `target="_blank"` and `window.open` is
denied. If the link was to an allowed page it opens in place instead, so nothing
appears broken.

**4. No navigating away.** Any attempt to move the page, a frame, or a redirect
to a non-allowlisted host is cancelled. Non-web schemes (`mailto:`, `steam:`,
`file:`) are refused, so no page can launch another program.

**5. No keyboard escapes, but games keep their keys.** A page-level filter
swallows modifier combinations, function keys, devtools and reload. A second
OS-level layer takes 64 shortcuts away from the window manager itself, including
`Cmd/Alt+Tab`, Mission Control and Spotlight.

What still reaches the game: **arrow keys, WASD and every other letter, the
digits, space, Enter, Escape, and Ctrl or Shift pressed on their own.** A
modifier held by itself is a game action; only a modifier *combined* with
another key is a shortcut. The page is given keyboard focus on load and whenever
it returns from the exit gate.

**6. Nothing else.** Downloads cancelled. Right-click, devtools and `alert()`
traps disabled. All permissions denied except fullscreen and pointer lock. No
app menu. Bad certificates never overridable. Its own browser profile, entirely
separate from yours.

## The window

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/the-window/

> Full screen, always on top, and how that differs on each operating system.

The app does **not** use native fullscreen, deliberately. On macOS a
native-fullscreen app gets its own Space, and a three-finger swipe slides
straight past it to the desktop.

Instead the window is frameless, fixed, sized to the whole display, and kept at
`screen-saver` level so it sits above the Dock and menu bar. On macOS it also
joins every Space, so swiping brings the window along rather than revealing
what is behind it.

A site that asks for fullscreen with its own button still gets it. The bar
slides away and **Esc** brings it back.

## Editing by hand

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/config-files/

> The configuration files, for anyone who would rather use a text editor.

Everything above writes to `catalog.json`, which you can edit directly if you prefer.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Unique short name, no spaces |
| `title` | Caption under the tile |
| `url` | The page that opens |
| `shape` | `star` `rocket` `ball` `blocks` `note` `leaf` `drop` `bolt` |
| `color` | Tile colour, `#rrggbb` |
| `allowHosts` | **Only** these hosts may load. `example.com` also covers `a.example.com`, never `evil-example.com` |
| `denyHosts` | Overrides `allowHosts`, for ad subdomains of an allowed domain |
| `blockAds` | `false` leaves the site's advertising alone |
| `enabled` | `true` to show the tile |

Check your work from a terminal:

```bash
npm run probe -- --probe=https://example.com   # what hosts does this site need?
npm run check -- --check=my-games              # does my profile actually work?
```

## What this cannot do

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/limits/

> The honest list of what Sukhi Play does not protect against, written down rather than glossed over.

**Blocked at the OS level while the app is in front:** `Cmd/Alt+Tab`, `F1`–`F20`,
Mission Control and Spaces, Spotlight, `Cmd/Ctrl+Q W M H N T R P S O F J L D U`,
devtools shortcuts, zoom, `Alt+F4`, and screen capture (`Print Screen` and its
variants, `Cmd+Shift+3/4/5/6`). Released the moment the window loses focus.

**Not blocked, on purpose:**

- **Force Quit.** `Cmd+Alt+Esc` on macOS, `Ctrl+Alt+Del` on Windows, and
  `Ctrl+Shift+Esc`. Left alone so the machine can always be recovered. Do not
  add these.

**Held a different way, because Windows will not hand it over:**

- **The Windows key.** A bare `Super` accelerator is rejected by Electron
  outright, and Windows refuses `Super+D`, `Super+E`, `Super+R`, `Super+L`,
  `Super+Tab`, `Super+Shift+S` and the rest when asked for them. Only
  `Super+V`, `Super+Plus` and `Super+-` are handed over, and those are taken.

  So pressing it opens the Start menu over the kiosk, and asking for focus back
  does nothing: Windows refuses a foreground request from a background process,
  and Start is drawn above every application window regardless of always-on-top.

  What works is Escape. While the lockdown is on, a PowerShell helper watches
  for the Start menu, Search and the quick settings panel, presses Escape on
  whichever appeared and brings the window back to the front, measured at about
  a quarter of a second. Any other foreground window is left alone, so keys are
  never sent into a dialog. The helper starts with the lockdown and stops with
  the app; nothing is installed and nothing on the machine is changed.

  Run `npm run start-probe` to watch it happen, and `npm run key-probe` to
  re-measure which keys this OS hands over.

**On Linux the desktop's own shortcuts are borrowed, not blocked.** Alt+Tab and
the Super key belong to GNOME rather than to any application, and under
**Wayland**, the default on current Ubuntu, an application cannot intercept keys
at all: Electron's global shortcuts are an X11 facility, and on Wayland they
report success and catch nothing.

So on a GNOME session Sukhi Play switches those bindings off in GNOME's own
settings while it runs, and puts them back exactly as they were when it quits.
25 of them, including Alt+Tab, the Super key, workspace switching and the
screenshot keys.

Every original value is written to disk before anything changes, so a crash
cannot leave you without Alt+Tab: the next start finds the backup and restores
from it. Set `borrowDesktopShortcuts` to `false` in `settings.json` if you would
rather it left your desktop alone.

On a desktop other than GNOME, choose **Xorg** at the login screen (the gear on
the password field) for the in-app layer to work at all. The app says which
session it found:

```
[gnome] borrowed 25 desktop shortcuts, including Alt+Tab and the Super key
[gnome] originals saved to ..., restored when this app quits
```

**Cannot be blocked by any application:**

- **Hardware media keys.** On a Mac, F-keys report as brightness, volume or
  Launchpad unless "Use F1, F2 as standard function keys" is on. The key never
  arrives as `F4`, so nothing can catch it.
- **Trackpad swipes between Spaces.** Handled by the window manager, never
  delivered to applications. The window follows onto the new Space, so your
  child still lands on Sukhi Play.

For a guarantee rather than a very good default, use a **separate user account**
for your child, or Windows **Assigned Access** (Settings → Accounts → Set up a
kiosk). Both are per-account and leave your own login untouched.

**This is not a substitute for supervision.** It reduces what a small child can
reach; it does not childproof a computer.

## If it ever locks you out

https://sukhiplay.com/docs/locked-out/

> Getting back in when the gate will not open, on every platform.

The app is built to **fail open**. If the launcher does not appear within 12
seconds, or its window crashes, everything unlocks by itself: the 64 keyboard
shortcuts are handed back for the rest of the session, always-on-top and screen
covering are switched off, the window becomes an ordinary one you can close, and
a plain message explains what happened. A kiosk with no visible exit gate must
not also be holding `Cmd+Q`.

If you still need to get out:

- **Force Quit.** `Cmd+Alt+Esc` on macOS, `Ctrl+Alt+Del` on Windows. Never
  captured, on purpose.
- **From a terminal**, if you can reach one: `pkill -f "Sukhi Play"`

When testing changes, give any run a hard deadline so it cannot take over the
machine:

```bash
SUKHI_EXIT_AFTER=15 npm start    # quits itself after 15 seconds
npm run dev                      # no screen covering, no shortcut capture
```

## Sukhi's Railway: a train set on the screen, and my first experiment

https://sukhiplay.com/blog/sukhis-railway-an-experiment/ (Announcements, 2026-09-26, by Mandeep Singh)

> A free track-building toy for ages three to five. It is an experiment: on the website only, not in Sukhi Play, until I know children love it.

- Sukhi's Railway is a free toy for children of about three to five: drag a finger to lay track, press Go, and Sukhi drives it.
- It is an experiment. It lives on the website only, not inside Sukhi Play, so it can change every week.
- It works on a phone, a tablet or a computer, needs no reading, and keeps working with no internet once opened.
- If your child tries it, tell me how it went. That decides whether it becomes a proper app.

My son had started to get bored of the colouring book. So I built him a
railway on the screen: a grass board, a tray of track, and a big green button.
He lays the track, presses Go, and a little version of him drives it round.

Then I showed it to him, and learned that building the track is the hard part.

## What it is

Drag a finger across the grass and track follows it, putting in the straights
and curves by itself. Press **Go** and Sukhi sets off, in a train, a car or a
bus.

![Sukhi's Railway on a phone, with the track turned upright to fit the screen and the controls below it](/screenshots/railway/02-on-a-phone.png "On a phone the board turns upright, so nothing is too small to press.")

Along the way there are pieces that do something:

| Piece | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Station | Animals wait on the platform, then climb aboard |
| Bridge | The wheels rattle and the water splashes |
| Tunnel | Dark for a moment, and Sukhi pulls a silly face |
| Ramp | A little jump, and a "wheee" |
| Bell | It swings and rings as he passes |
| Car wash | Bubbles, everywhere |

There is a tortoise for slow and a hare for fast, an undo button that is
always there, and every track saves itself under **My tracks**. No reading, no
losing, nothing to buy.

## Why it is an experiment

When I showed it to my son, who is not yet four, laying the track was hard
for him to understand. I think part of that is the device: he tried it on one
he does not usually play on, and I expect him to work it out better on his
own. But one child, one try, is not enough to know.

So instead of putting it inside Sukhi Play, where every change waits for a
release, it lives on the website, in a new **Experiments** section of the
[playground](/playground/#experiments). Any child can try it there, and I can
change it every week as I learn.

## Try it with your child

Open [sukhiplay.com/playground/railway](/playground/railway/) on whatever they
usually play on. On a phone or tablet, add it to the home screen and it opens
full screen, like any other app.

Then watch where they get stuck, and [tell me on GitHub](https://github.com/meSingh/sukhi-play/issues):
their age, the device, and whether they asked for it again. "It did not work
for us" helps as much as "they loved it".

If it sticks, it becomes a proper app in Sukhi Play. If it does not, it changes,
or it goes.

**Is Sukhi's Railway in Sukhi Play?** Not yet. It is on the website only, at sukhiplay.com/playground/railway/. If children keep coming back to it, it gets a release inside Sukhi Play.

**What age is Sukhi's Railway for?** About three to five. Pressing Go and watching needs nothing at all; laying track needs a little more, and finding the age where that clicks is part of the experiment.

**Does it work without internet?** Yes, once it has been opened once. Tracks are kept in that browser on that device, and nothing is sent anywhere.

## Parental controls or a locked-down browser for an under-five?

https://sukhiplay.com/blog/parental-controls-vs-kiosk-browser/ (For parents, 2026-09-26, by Mandeep Singh)

> Parental controls filter what an older child finds online. An under-five needs containment: one screen, only the sites you chose, and no way out.

Parental controls and content filters are built to keep an older child away from bad content while they browse on their own. An under-five has a different problem: they cannot read, they tap everything, and one wrong tap takes them off the page. What they need is containment, a single screen with only the things you chose and no way out, which is what a locked-down (kiosk) browser does.

The two are not rivals. They solve different problems, and plenty of families end up using both.

## What do parental controls actually do?

Most parental controls are a mix of four things:

- **Content filters.** Block categories of website, such as adult content or gambling, and turn on safe search.
- **Time limits.** A daily allowance, or hours when the device is off.
- **Approvals.** A grown-up says yes before an app is installed or something is bought.
- **Reports.** What was used, and for how long.

Good ones are built into everything already: Screen Time on Apple devices, Microsoft's family settings on Windows, Google Family Link on Android, and filtering in many home routers and broadband packages.

They share an assumption: the child is using the device the way a grown-up does. They open a browser, go places, search. The filter's job is to catch the bad places. Everything else is allowed.

## Why does a toddler need something different?

Because a three-year-old is not browsing. They are pressing things to see what happens.

- **They cannot read**, so an advert and a game's play button look the same.
- **They tap everything**, including "skip", "install", "open in app" and the tiny cross that is really part of the advert.
- **They escape the page**, with the back button, a closed window or a palm on the keyboard.
- **Autoplay decides what comes next.** On video sites, the next thing is chosen for them.
- **Adverts appear on perfectly respectable sites**, and a content filter has no reason to block a respectable site.

None of this is inappropriate content, so a filter lets all of it through. The toddler still ends up somewhere they cannot get back from, upset, or on your email.

## What is a kiosk browser?

A browser that starts from "nothing" instead of "everything". It covers the screen, has no address bar or tabs, shows only what you listed, and needs a grown-up to close.

In Sukhi Play that means six layers, described in full in [how the lockdown works](/docs/lockdown/):

1. each site may only load from the hosts you allowed, so ad networks nobody has heard of are blocked simply because they are not on the list
2. a blocklist of known ad and tracker domains, checked even on allowed sites
3. no popups or new windows
4. no navigating to anywhere off the list
5. keyboard shortcuts taken away while it is in front, while game keys still work
6. no downloads, no right-click, and its own browser profile, separate from yours

## How do parental controls and a kiosk browser compare?

| | Parental controls | Kiosk browser |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starts from | Everything allowed, known bad blocked | Nothing allowed, your choices let in |
| Built for | Children who read and browse | Children who cannot read yet |
| Adverts | Usually not their job | Filtered, and cannot lead off the page |
| Leaving the page | Allowed | Refused |
| Shortcuts and desktop | Untouched | Taken away while it is in front |
| Time limits | Usually per day | Sukhi Play: per session |
| Grows with the child | Yes | Outgrown once they read |

## When is each the right choice?

A kiosk browser fits when:

- your child is under five or so, and does not read yet
- they use two or three sites, not the whole web
- the computer is a shared laptop with your work on it

Parental controls fit when:

- your child reads and searches for things on purpose
- they have their own device or account
- you want reports, or limits across every app

In between, there are good built-in options. On an iPad, Guided Access locks the screen to one app. For videos, YouTube Kids is a much better fit than YouTube, which Sukhi Play deliberately leaves out of its catalogue.

## Can I use both together?

Yes, and for a small child on a shared computer it is the strongest setup:

1. **A separate account for your child,** so your files and logins are not behind whatever they are doing.
2. **Parental controls on that account,** for time limits and anything outside the browser.
3. **A kiosk browser as the thing they use,** so they stay on the screen you chose.

The Sukhi Play docs recommend a separate user account, or Windows Assigned Access, for anyone who wants a guarantee rather than a very good default.

## What does a kiosk browser not do?

It is only fair to say. Sukhi Play does not judge whether a site you add is suitable; it only makes sure nothing else loads. It does not keep a daily total or send you reports. The Force Quit keys are left working so the machine can always be recovered, and on Windows the Start menu can flash up before the app closes it. [What this cannot do](/docs/limits/) lists the rest.

And neither kind of tool replaces a grown-up in the room. They reduce what a small child can reach. They do not childproof a computer.

If a kiosk browser sounds right, [how I set up Sukhi Play for my three-year-old](/blog/setting-up-sukhi-play-for-a-toddler/) is a good place to start, and [the download page](/download/) has it for macOS, Windows and Linux, free.

**Do I still need parental controls if I use a kiosk browser?** Not for what happens inside it, because only the sites you added can load. They are still worth having on the child's account for everything outside it, such as other apps and the time spent on the computer overall.

**Is a kiosk browser suitable for an older child?** It is safe, but it quickly becomes too small. Once a child reads and wants to search for things, parental controls and a conversation about what they find do more good than a screen of six tiles.

**Does Sukhi Play block adverts?** Yes. Advert and tracker requests are cut before they load on every site you add. A few sites ask in their terms not to be filtered, and you can leave those alone; your child still cannot leave the site.

**Can a toddler get out of a kiosk browser?** Not by tapping or by the usual shortcuts. The Force Quit keys are left working on purpose so a grown-up can always recover the computer, and on Windows the Start menu can appear for a moment before it is closed.

## Printable name labels, stickers and bookmarks for children

https://sukhiplay.com/blog/printables-for-kids-at-home/ (For parents, 2026-09-26, by Mandeep Singh)

> Jazz's Studio is a free stationery maker for children of seven and up: name labels, stickers, bookmarks, gift tags and door signs, each on one A4 page.

My daughter Jazz is ten and loves stationery, so I made her a studio where she designs her own name labels, stickers, bookmarks, gift tags and door signs, and prints them at home. It is called Jazz's Studio, it is free, it runs in any browser at [sukhiplay.com/playground/studio](/playground/studio/) with no account, and every sheet prints on one A4 page from an ordinary home printer.

Your child can use all of it, with their own name on everything and, if they like, their own character in place of Jazz's.

## What can children make and print at home?

The **Stationery** part of the studio has five groups:

- **Stickers:** "me stickers" of their character in different poses, or pattern stickers in circles, squares and hexagons to cut out.
- **Diary:** a cover with their name and character on it, and pages with the date, a mood and lines to write on.
- **Labels and tags:** name labels for books, boxes and pencil cases, and gift tags for presents.
- **Planners and lists:** a week planner, and one to four to-do lists on a page with boxes to tick.
- **Bookmarks and signs:** bookmarks, four to a page, and door signs that hang on a door handle.

Each sheet keeps its own colours, lettering and pattern, so changing the bookmark does not change the stickers. Beyond stationery there are wraps to turn a toilet roll or a cereal box into a pencil pot or desk tidy, a logo for each person with business cards and logo stickers, a name poster, secret messages in a real code, and a story page to write and draw. [The studio page](/studio/) shows it all.

## Who is it for?

Children of about seven and up. It was made for a ten-year-old, and most of it involves typing words and choosing between options, so it suits a child who reads. For younger children, [Sukhi Colouring](/colouring/) needs no reading at all.

## How do I make name labels for school things?

1. Open the studio and choose **Stationery**, then **Labels and tags**, then **Name labels**.
2. Type the name. The line above it starts as "This belongs to", and you can change it.
3. Pick the colours and lettering, and whether their character goes on.
4. Print, and cut the labels out.

A sheet can hold several people, each with their own name, which is handy with brothers and sisters.

Be realistic about where paper labels go. They are good on books, folders, pencil cases and boxes. They will not survive a washing machine or a dishwasher, so clothes and lunchboxes need proper labels made for that.

## Do I need special sticker paper?

No. Plain printer paper works for everything: cut the shapes out and use a glue stick or clear tape. A strip of clear tape over a name label on a book cover also makes it last much longer.

If you want real stickers, the easy choice is whole-sheet sticker paper: one big sticky sheet that you print on and cut up yourself, so nothing has to line up with pre-cut shapes. Two things to check on the packet:

- that it is made for your kind of printer, inkjet or laser
- that your printer can take it (the printer's manual lists the paper it accepts)

For bookmarks and door signs, thicker paper or thin card works best, if your printer will feed it. Covering a bookmark with clear tape on both sides makes a paper one survive a school bag.

## How do I get it to print on one page?

Everything is drawn on A4 to the millimetre and prints on one page, and nothing sits closer than 10 mm to the edge, so printers that cannot print right to the edge are fine.

- **Box wraps** from Make from a box should be printed at **actual size** (100%), not "fit to page", so they fit the thing you measured. Each wrap has a line that should measure exactly 5 cm, so a ruler can check.
- **On an iPad**, Safari adds the address and date at the top and bottom, and always prints a little smaller than actual size. That is fine for stickers and labels; for a wrap, measure the 5 cm line.
- **If your printer uses US Letter paper**, look at the print preview before printing, because the sheets are drawn for A4.

## Ideas for gift tags, bookmarks and door signs

- **Gift tags** come eight to a sheet. Punch a hole and thread ribbon or string through. Leave the "To" and "From" empty and they can be written in by hand.
- **Bookmarks** with their name, or a friend's, down the middle make a good small present.
- **Door signs** come two to a sheet, shaped to hang on a door handle, with their own words on them.
- **Kept prints** mean next term's labels are one press away. After printing, the studio offers to keep the print in **My makes**, and opening it later brings the sheet back exactly as it was.

## Where are their designs kept?

On that device only. Nothing is uploaded and there is no account. Clearing the browser's data for the site, or using a private window, clears it too.

To keep it on a phone or tablet, open it and use **Add to Home Screen**. Once it has been opened, it works without internet. [Jazz's Studio in the docs](/docs/jazz-studio/) has the details.

## Can I use it inside Sukhi Play?

Yes. It comes in the [Sukhi Play](/download/) download but switched off, so a younger child's screen stays as it was. Open the grown-up screen, go to the catalogue and add **Studio**.

Inside Sukhi Play there is no print window, because a print window can save a file or open another program, both ways out of a locked screen. The page goes straight to the computer's default printer, and the studio tells your child when it has gone, or to ask a grown-up if the printer did not answer.

The [announcement for Jazz's Studio](/blog/jazzs-studio/) tells the story of why I made it.

**Is Jazz's Studio free?** Yes. There is no account, no adverts and nothing to buy, and in a browser there is nothing to install either.

**What age is it for?** About seven and up, because most of it means typing words and choosing between options. Younger children usually get more from Sukhi Colouring, which needs no reading at all.

**Can my child put their own character on the stickers?** Yes. In Make it yours, Add a character takes a picture of a character on one plain colour, cuts the background out on the device and asks who it is. Nothing added to the studio leaves the device, though if you use Google Gemini to make a character from a photo, that photo goes to Google.

**Why did my box wrap print the wrong size?** It was probably scaled to fit the page. Print it at actual size, or 100%, then measure the 5 cm line on the wrap with a ruler. An iPad always prints a little smaller than actual size.

**Does it work on a phone or tablet?** Yes. Open it in the browser and use Add to Home Screen to keep it there; it works without internet once it has been opened. It prints from a phone or tablet too, on one A4 page.

## Screen time for a three-year-old: the guidance and what works

https://sukhiplay.com/blog/screen-time-three-year-old/ (For parents, 2026-09-26, by Mandeep Singh)

> The WHO says no more than an hour of sedentary screen time a day for ages two to four, and less is better. Short sessions and a calm stop make it workable.

The World Health Organization says children aged two to four should have no more than one hour of sedentary screen time a day, and that less is better. The American Academy of Pediatrics gives the same hour for ages two to five, of high-quality programmes, watched together where possible. What made that workable for me was less the number than the shape: short sessions, the same calm stop every time, and sites that do not shout.

This is one parent's experience, not medical advice. If you are worried about your child, your GP or health visitor is the person to ask.

## What does the WHO say about screen time for a three-year-old?

The WHO's 2019 guidelines for children under five put it simply. For ages two to four, sedentary screen time should be no more than one hour a day, and less is better. For children under two it is not recommended at all.

The guidance is as much about moving, playing and sleeping as it is about screens. Screens are counted as time spent sitting still, and the message is to sit less and play more. The [WHO news release](https://www.who.int/news/item/24-04-2019-to-grow-up-healthy-children-need-to-sit-less-and-play-more) is short and worth reading in full.

## What does the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend?

For children aged two to five, the AAP suggests limiting screen use to about one hour a day of high-quality programming, and watching it with them where you can, so you can talk about what they are seeing. Their [advice for parents](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/family-life/Media/Pages/Where-We-Stand-TV-Viewing-Time.aspx) is on HealthyChildren.org.

## Is one hour of screen time too much for a three-year-old?

An hour is a ceiling, not a target. Both sets of guidance say less is better, and neither says a child needs screens at all.

What matters as much in practice is what the time looks like. Twenty calm minutes with a grown-up nearby is a very different thing from an hour of something fast and loud, alone.

## Is it better to have one long session or a few short ones?

Short sessions, for a child this age. A three-year-old has no idea what "twenty minutes left today" means. A session, on the other hand, has a beginning and an end they can see: they sit down, they play, the screen says it is finished, they get up.

It also makes the stop predictable. If every session is the same length, the end stops being a surprise and starts being a routine.

## How do I warn a toddler that screen time is nearly over?

With your voice, tied to something they understand. "When this picture is finished" or "after this one" lands better than a number.

A countdown on the screen tends to do the opposite of what you want. It gives a child something to watch, and something to bargain with. That is why Sukhi Play shows no countdown at all until the last thirty seconds.

## How do I end screen time without a meltdown?

There is no trick that works every time, but these helped:

1. **Let the stop come from the screen, not from you.** A stop screen that simply says play is over is hard to argue with, because there is nobody to argue with.
2. **Keep the length the same every time.** Consistency does most of the work.
3. **Have the next thing ready.** A snack, the garden, the bath. Ending is easier when it is also starting something.
4. **Do not give more time on demand.** If you do give more, make it clearly your decision, not the result of a good argument.
5. **Sit with them when you can.** Both for the reasons the AAP gives, and because you see the stop coming.

## Which sites are calmer for small children?

Look for things a child makes, rather than things that play at them:

- no autoplay, and no "up next"
- no adverts
- no timers, streaks or flashing rewards
- nothing that needs reading to get started

Colouring, drawing, building and simple music toys tend to end more gently than videos, because there is no cliffhanger. If your child does watch videos, YouTube Kids is a better starting point than YouTube, and has parental settings of its own.

## What free tools can end a session for me?

Several are built in. On an iPad, Guided Access has a time limit option, and Screen Time can set limits on Apple devices. On Windows, Microsoft's family settings can limit screen time on a child's account, and Google Family Link does the same on Android.

## How does Sukhi Play's play time work?

On a laptop or desktop, [Sukhi Play](/download/) does this as part of the locked-down screen. On the grown-up screen's **Play time** tab, you set a session length once: any number of minutes up to four hours, or no limit. The clock starts again every time the app opens.

Your child sees no countdown until the last thirty seconds. When the time is up, a stop screen says "That is all for now" and nothing else will open. They can ask for more, but only a grown-up can answer: fifteen minutes, an hour, or the rest of the day, for that session only. Your usual limit does not move.

It is honest to say it counts a session, not a day. Close it and open it again after lunch and the clock starts fresh, so keeping the daily total is still your job. [Play time in the docs](/docs/play-time/) has the detail, and [the announcement](/blog/play-time-limits/) explains why it works this way.

If you are setting it up for the first time, [how I set up Sukhi Play for my three-year-old](/blog/setting-up-sukhi-play-for-a-toddler/) covers the first few sessions.

**Do educational apps count as screen time?** The WHO guideline is about sedentary screen time, whatever is on the screen, so yes. Choosing good content matters a great deal, but it does not make the hour longer.

**Should I let my child finish the game when time runs out?** In Sukhi Play the stop screen arrives when the time is up, whatever is happening. If finishing a level matters to your child, give your spoken warning early enough for them to finish, or grant fifteen minutes yourself from the stop screen.

**Does Sukhi Play keep a daily total?** No. The clock starts again from your rule every time the app opens, and nothing is stored between runs. That keeps it simple for a small child, but the daily total is yours to keep.

**Is it all right if my three-year-old has no screen time at all?** Nothing in either guideline says a child needs screens. Less is better, and none is a perfectly good amount.

## How I set up Sukhi Play for my three-year-old

https://sukhiplay.com/blog/setting-up-sukhi-play-for-a-toddler/ (For parents, 2026-09-26, by Mandeep Singh)

> Start with two or three tiles, sit beside them for the first sessions, set a short play time and add sites slowly. The setup I would repeat, step by step.

Keep the first screen small: two or three tiles, a short play time, and you sitting beside them for the first few sessions. Show them the stop screen early so it becomes normal, change the way in if they learn it, and add sites one at a time as they grow. That is roughly how I set Sukhi Play up for my son, and what I would do again.

Sukhi was around three when I built it. He pressed every key and clicked every button, which on a normal laptop means adverts, popups, new tabs and eventually my work. Here is the setup, in the order I would do it.

## What do I need before I start?

A Mac, a Windows PC or a Linux computer, and a few minutes. It is free, with no account and nothing to sign up for. The installers are on [the download page](/download/).

The builds are signed but not notarised, so the first launch shows a warning on macOS and on Windows. [Installing](/docs/installing/) walks through getting past it, once per install.

## How does the first run work?

The first time it opens, it asks who is using the computer. Choose **I'm a grown-up** and it walks you through four short steps:

1. What your child will and will not be able to reach.
2. Choose what they can open.
3. How you get back out, with a chance to practise the three-second hold.
4. Hand it over.

Do practise the hold. You want to know the feel of it before a small person is waiting. [The first run](/docs/first-run/) has the detail.

## How many sites should a three-year-old start with?

Two or three. More than that and a small child hops from tile to tile without settling on anything.

Three apps come switched on already, and for a three-year-old they are a reasonable first screen on their own:

- **Colouring**, Sukhi Colouring, with forty pictures to colour or a blank page
- **Keyboard**, Magic Smash by Evandro Meneses, where pressing any key makes something happen
- **First Games**, Little Explorer by pazarman, with counting, colours, shapes and animals and no reading needed

All three live inside the download, so they work offline and have no adverts. The tiles are big, bright and marked with simple shapes, so your child does not need to read to choose one. [What your child sees](/docs/what-child-sees/) shows the rest.

## Which sites should I keep off at first?

Anything that asks more of a small child than tapping:

- **Games that need reading** to get past a menu or understand the rules.
- **Autoplay video.** youtube.com is deliberately not in the catalogue for this reason.
- **Sites with adverts.** The catalogue labels each site no ads, ads filtered or ads showing, so you can choose.
- **Logins, chat and purchases.** None of these belong on a toddler's screen.
- **Anything fast, loud or timed.** Those tend to make the stop harder.

## Should I sit with them the first time?

Yes, for the first few sessions. Show them the tiles, and the big blue **Back** button at the top of every site that takes them home. Let them press the small ✕ and see that nothing happens without a grown-up.

You will also learn which sites actually work for your child. One that looked lovely on the list may start with a menu they cannot read.

## How long should play time be?

Short, to begin with. On the grown-up screen's **Play time** tab, pick a length once and it applies every time the app opens. There are shortcuts from ten minutes to an hour, or you can type any number up to four hours.

Your child sees no countdown until the last thirty seconds. [Screen time for a three-year-old](/blog/screen-time-three-year-old/) has what the WHO and the American Academy of Pediatrics suggest, and [play time](/docs/play-time/) has how it works.

## How do I make the stop screen feel normal?

Let an early session end on it while you are there. It says "That is all for now", and nothing else will open.

Your child can press **Ask for more time**, but only you can answer, with fifteen minutes, an hour or the rest of the day, for that session only. If you do not want to give more, there is a button for a grown-up to close Sukhi Play from the same screen. It works best when the answer is usually no. The stop is then just what happens, not the start of a discussion.

## What if my child learns the grown-up hold?

They might. A toddler does not manage a three-second hold by accident, but one who uses the app every day learns it eventually, and mine did.

When that happens, open **Settings** and switch **Getting in here** from *Hold* to *Sum*. You are then asked a small addition instead, and holding the button stops doing anything at all. Three wrong answers in a row lock the gate for ten seconds. [The grown-up gate](/docs/the-gate/) has the rest.

## How do I add sites as they grow?

Open **Grown-ups** and hold for three seconds, then:

- **From the catalogue:** tap a site and it arrives on the tile screen with everything it needs already filled in. The same list is on [the catalogue page](/catalogue/).
- **Any other site:** type its address. Sukhi Play opens it once, watches what it loads, and works out what to allow. Give the tile a name, a shape and a colour, and press **Save**.

Each app has a switch on its card, so you can take a tile away for a while without deleting it. [Adding and removing sites](/docs/adding-sites/) covers it all.

Jazz's Studio, the stationery app I made for my daughter, waits in the catalogue too. It is for children of about seven and up, so leave it off for now.

## What will it not do?

It is not a substitute for being nearby. The Force Quit keys are left working on purpose so you can always recover the computer, and on Windows the Start menu can appear for a moment before the app closes it. [What this cannot do](/docs/limits/) is the honest list, and [how to let a toddler use your laptop](/blog/toddler-laptop-without-losing-work/) covers the habits that go with it.

**Which apps are switched on when Sukhi Play is first installed?** Three that come inside the download: Sukhi Colouring, a keyboard playground called Magic Smash, and a set of first games called Little Explorer. They are files on your own computer, so they work without internet.

**Can I hide a tile without deleting it?** Yes. On the grown-up screen each app has a switch in the corner of its card. Turn it off and the tile leaves your child's screen, with everything about it kept for later.

**What happens if the tile screen is empty?** It says so plainly and offers a button that takes you to the grown-up screen, where you can switch an app on or add one.

**Can I start the setup again from scratch?** Yes. Reset Sukhi Play to factory settings, on the Settings tab, restarts into the walkthrough. It wipes every app and setting, asks twice, and cannot be undone.

## Why toddlers bash the keyboard, and a safe place to let them

https://sukhiplay.com/blog/toddler-keyboard-smashing/ (For parents, 2026-09-26, by Mandeep Singh)

> Toddlers bash keys because every press does something and they copy you. On a normal computer that hits shortcuts; a locked-down screen makes it safe.

Toddlers bash the keyboard because every press makes something happen, and because they have watched you use it all day. On a normal computer those presses land on shortcuts that close windows, switch apps and change settings. The answer is not to take the keyboard away, but to give them a screen where pressing everything is safe.

My son Sukhi, at around three, pressed every key and clicked every button he could reach. Sukhi Play started as a screen where pressing all of them was fine.

## Why does my toddler bash the keyboard?

No study needed for this one, just a few afternoons of watching:

- **Cause and effect.** Press a key, something changes. A keyboard has more buttons than anything else in the house, and they all click.
- **Copying you.** They have seen grown-ups typing for as long as they can remember. The keyboard is obviously where the important things happen.
- **Whole hands.** A small child does not press one key. They press five, with a flat palm, often twice.

That last one is the problem.

## Why is keyboard bashing risky on a normal computer?

Because shortcuts are combinations, and a palm on the keyboard makes combinations all the time. A few that toddlers find without trying:

- **Cmd+W or Ctrl+W** closes the tab, and **Cmd+Q** or **Alt+F4** closes the whole program.
- **Cmd+Tab or Alt+Tab** switches to whatever else you had open.
- **The Windows key** opens the Start menu.
- **Ctrl+P or Cmd+P** starts printing.
- **Shift pressed five times** on Windows asks about turning on Sticky Keys.

A silicone keyboard cover does not help here. It keeps crumbs out, but every key underneath still presses.

## What is a safe way to let a toddler bash the keyboard?

For free, with nothing to install: open a blank document, make the text enormous, and let them press away while you sit next to them. Letters appear, which is exactly the point, and you can name them as they go. The catch is that every shortcut still works, so you have to be the lockdown.

An old keyboard that is not plugged into anything is also a perfectly good toy for copying you.

If you want them to play on their own, the keys themselves need to be made safe.

## How does Sukhi Play make keyboard bashing safe?

Two layers, described in [how the lockdown works](/docs/lockdown/):

1. **Inside the page**, a filter swallows modifier combinations, function keys, developer tools and reload.
2. **At the operating system**, while the app is in front, it takes 64 shortcuts away from the computer itself, including Cmd+Tab and Alt+Tab, Mission Control, Spotlight, the common Cmd and Ctrl shortcuts such as Q, W, T, N and P, Alt+F4, the function keys, zoom and screenshots.

What still reaches the game is what a game needs: arrow keys, every letter, the digits, space, Enter, Escape, and Ctrl or Shift pressed on their own. A modifier held by itself is a game action. Only a modifier combined with another key counts as a shortcut, so leaning on Ctrl and W together closes nothing.

## What can Sukhi Play not block?

Some keys belong to the computer, not to any app. [What this cannot do](/docs/limits/) is the full list, but for a keyboard-basher these are the ones to know:

- **Force Quit** (Cmd+Option+Esc on a Mac, Ctrl+Alt+Delete or Ctrl+Shift+Esc on Windows) is left alone on purpose, so a grown-up can always recover the machine. These open a window rather than closing anything, but you may need to press Cancel.
- **The Windows key** opens the Start menu over the app. Sukhi Play closes the Start menu, Search and quick settings as soon as they appear, in about a quarter of a second, but Windows keeps its own Windows-key combinations for itself.
- **A Mac's top row** controls brightness and volume unless it is set to act as standard function keys. No app can catch those, so set the volume and brightness first.
- **On Linux**, Sukhi Play switches off the desktop's own Alt+Tab and Super key while it runs on GNOME, and puts them back afterwards. On other desktops, choose an Xorg session for its keyboard layer to work, and note the Snap version does not do this at all.

And no app can stop someone pressing the power button.

## Is there something inside Sukhi Play made for bashing keys?

Yes. The **Keyboard** tile, switched on from the start, is **Magic Smash**, an open-source keyboard playground by Evandro Meneses that comes inside the download. Press any key and something happens: the key appears big on the screen with a burst of colour, and a gentle sound if you have it on, in themes from space to the ocean to animals.

It works with no internet and has no adverts, because it is a set of files on your own computer. Next to it are **First Games**, Little Explorer by pazarman, with counting, colours, shapes and animals and no reading needed, and **Colouring**, the colouring book that comes with Sukhi Play. [The catalogue](/catalogue/) lists all of them.

## A few habits that help

1. **Save and close your own work first.** Always, whatever is running.
2. **Turn the volume down** before a keyboard game, not after.
3. **Sit with them the first few times.** Naming the letters they press turns bashing into a game you play together.
4. **Keep drinks well away.**

For the wider picture, [how to let a toddler use your laptop without losing your work](/blog/toddler-laptop-without-losing-work/) covers separate accounts and the rest, and [how I set up Sukhi Play for my three-year-old](/blog/setting-up-sukhi-play-for-a-toddler/) goes through the first sessions. It is free for macOS, Windows and Linux on [the download page](/download/).

**Can my toddler close Sukhi Play by bashing the keyboard?** Not with the usual shortcuts; closing needs a button held for three seconds. The Force Quit keys are left working on purpose so a grown-up can always recover the computer, but they open a window of options rather than closing anything by themselves.

**Does the keyboard playground need the internet?** No. Magic Smash comes inside the download as files on your own computer, so it works offline and has no adverts.

**Why does the Start menu flash up on Windows?** Windows will not hand the Windows key to an application. Sukhi Play watches for the Start menu, closes it and brings its own window back, in about a quarter of a second.

**Can my toddler change the brightness or volume on a Mac?** Yes. The top row of keys controls brightness and volume unless they are set to act as standard function keys, and no app can catch them. Set both before you hand the laptop over.

## How to let a toddler use your laptop without losing your work

https://sukhiplay.com/blog/toddler-laptop-without-losing-work/ (For parents, 2026-09-26, by Mandeep Singh)

> Give them a space your work is not in: their own user account, a locked-down browser with only the sites you chose, and your work saved and closed first.

- A toddler does not press one key, they press six with a flat hand. That is how shortcuts that close, send and delete get made.
- A separate user account keeps your files, email and logins out of reach. It is free and built in.
- A locked-down browser keeps the child inside the sites you chose, which an account alone does not.
- Both together is the safest setup, and saving and closing your own work first still matters most.

My son was three and wanted to play games on my laptop. He also clicked every
button on the screen, which meant adverts, popups, new tabs, and eventually my
work. He was not being naughty. He was pressing things, which is what
three-year-olds are for.

The fix is not to watch harder. It is to give them a space your work is not in.

## What a toddler actually does to a laptop

A small child does not press one key. They press a handful at once with a flat
palm, and that is exactly how keyboard shortcuts are made. Without meaning to,
they will:

- **close** a tab, a window, or the document you had not saved
- **send** a half-written email, or post a half-written message
- **delete** or drag away files
- **change** the brightness, the volume, the keyboard language
- **leave**, by tapping an advert that looked like a play button

## Your options, side by side

| Option | Protects your work | Keeps them on the right sites | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Full screen, and you sit with them | No | Until one press of Escape | Free |
| A separate user account | Yes | No | Free, built in |
| Windows kiosk mode (Assigned Access) | Yes | One app only | Free, on Pro and above |
| A locked-down browser like Sukhi Play | Mostly | Yes | Free |
| An account **and** a locked-down browser | Yes | Yes | Free |

### A separate user account

If you do one thing, do this. On a Mac, add a **Standard** user under Users &
Groups in System Settings. On Windows, add another account under Accounts in
Settings. Log in to it before you hand the laptop over, and your files, email
and saved logins are not there to break.

What an account does not do is keep a child anywhere. Inside it they can still
open any app, wander the web and tap every advert. It is a wall around your
things, not a fence around them.

### A locked-down browser

This is the fence. Sukhi Play fills the screen with big tiles for the sites you
picked, and nothing else opens: each site can only load what it needs, popups
and downloads are refused, and the shortcuts that close and switch apps are
taken away while it is in front.

![Sukhi Play asking a grown-up to hold a button for three seconds before it will close](/screenshots/05-closing-needs-a-grownup.png "Closing it takes a button held for three seconds. Every tap a toddler makes is a quick one.")

It is honest about its limits. The keys to force an app to quit are left alone
on purpose, so a computer can always be recovered, and nothing stops a finger
on the power button. [The full list](/docs/limits/) is written down.

## The safest setup

1. A **separate account** for your child, with nothing of yours signed in.
2. **Sukhi Play** in that account, with three or four sites they know.
3. A **play time** limit, so the screen ends the session and you do not have to.
4. Your own work **saved and closed** before you switch accounts.

If they ever get past the app, what is behind it is their account, not yours.

## Habits that matter more than any setting

- Close anything with a **Send** button before you hand it over.
- Set the **volume and brightness** first. Those keys belong to the computer.
- Keep **drinks** on the other side of the table.
- **Sit nearby** the first few times. Five minutes of watching teaches you more
  than any guide, this one included.

When you want to go further, [how I set up Sukhi Play for my three-year-old](/blog/setting-up-sukhi-play-for-a-toddler/)
covers the first week, and Sukhi Play itself is a [free download](/download/)
for macOS, Windows and Linux.

**Is a keyboard cover enough to protect my laptop from a toddler?** It keeps crumbs and juice out, but every key underneath still presses, so every shortcut still works. It protects the keyboard, not your work.

**Can a toddler delete files from a separate user account?** Only their own. A standard account cannot reach another account's files, so your documents, email and saved logins are simply not there.

**What if my child still gets out of the locked-down browser?** Every computer keeps a way to force an app to quit, on purpose. In Sukhi Play that key is left alone, so run it inside the child's own account and whatever is behind it is theirs, not yours.

**Does this work on a Chromebook?** Sukhi Play does not run on ChromeOS. A supervised child account through Google Family Link is the closest built-in option there.

Sources:
- Change Users & Groups settings on Mac (Apple): https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/add-a-user-or-group-mtusr001/mac
- Manage user accounts in Windows (Microsoft): https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/account-billing/create-a-local-user-or-administrator-account-in-windows-20de74e0-ac7f-3502-a866-32915af2a34d
- Assigned Access overview, Windows kiosk mode (Microsoft): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/configuration/assigned-access/
- Use Guided Access on iPhone or iPad (Apple): https://support.apple.com/en-us/111795

## Jazz's Studio: stationery to design and print, for ages 7 and up

https://sukhiplay.com/blog/jazzs-studio/ (Announcements, 2026-09-24, by Mandeep Singh)

> Jazz's Studio, new in Sukhi Play 2.2 and grown up in 2.3, lets children of seven and up design and print their own stickers, labels, diaries and more.

Jazz's Studio is a stationery studio for children of about seven and up: they design stickers, labels, bookmarks, gift tags, door signs and diaries with their own name and characters on them, and print them at home. It arrived in Sukhi Play 2.2.0 and grew up in 2.3.0. It is free, works without internet, and also runs in any browser at [sukhiplay.com/playground/studio](/playground/studio/).

## Why I made it

Sukhi Play started for my son, Sukhi, who is under four and presses every key and clicks everything. His sister Jazz is ten and loves stationery, so I made her a studio, and it has her name on it.

It is the first thing in Sukhi Play for older children, and yours can use all of it.

## What can children make in Jazz's Studio?

- **Stationery**, in five groups: stickers, a diary cover and pages, name labels and gift tags, a week planner and to-do lists, and bookmarks and door signs. Each sheet keeps its own colours, lettering and pattern.
- **Make from a box**: pick a pencil pot, desk tidy, notebook cover or treasure box, measure the toilet roll or cereal box, and print a wrap that fits it, with the steps.
- **My brand**: a logo for each person, as a badge, stamp, ribbon or tag, with business cards and logo stickers cut out round the logo's shape.
- **Play**: a poster of their name, secret messages in a real code with a key for a friend, story pages, a doodle pad, and invite cards.
- **My makes**: their prints, kept to open again, and a shelf of the things they made, each with a photo and a note.
- **Make it yours**: their character, their name, and the studio's colours, lettering and background.

## What is new in 2.3?

2.2.0 brought the studio into Sukhi Play. 2.3.0, out the same day, made it properly anyone's.

- **It asks who they are.** The first time it opens, it asks the child's name and their character, so nobody else is greeted as Jazz. Both can be skipped and changed later.
- **Sukhi joins Jazz**, with seven characters of his own.
- **Families add their own characters.** A picture of a character on one plain colour goes in, the background is cut out on the device, and the studio asks who it is. Each person has their own pictures, their own name and their own brand, and can be switched off without losing them.
- **Everyone on one sheet.** Stickers, labels, bookmarks, gift tags, door signs and box wraps take several people at once, each with their own words.
- **Invite cards.** Eight to a sheet, each with a QR code a friend's phone camera opens the studio from. The code is made on the device, with their character in the middle of it.
- **Story pages.** Who, what happens and where, chosen or spun, printed with a box to draw in and lines to write on.

## Keeping a print to use again

After a print, the studio asks whether to keep it in **My makes** and what to call it. It keeps the settings rather than a picture, so **Open** brings the sheet back exactly as it was, ready to print again or to change a word first.

## How does printing work?

Every sheet is drawn on A4 to the millimetre and prints on one page, on any printer, an iPad included. Print box wraps at actual size, not "fit to page"; each has a line that should measure exactly 5 cm. An iPad always prints a little smaller, which is fine for stickers but worth measuring for a wrap.

**Inside Sukhi Play there is no print window.** A print window can save a file or open another program, and both are ways out of the locked screen. So Sukhi Play sends the page straight to the computer's default printer, and the studio tells your child when it has gone, or to ask a grown-up if the printer did not answer. Only apps Sukhi Play made itself can print; a website that tries is refused.

## Where do I find it?

- **In Sukhi Play** it comes in the download but is switched off, so a younger child's screen stays as it was. Open the grown-up screen, go to its catalogue, and add **Studio** ([how](/docs/jazz-studio/)). It works with no internet at all.
- **On any other device**, open [/playground/studio/](/playground/studio/) in a browser. Nothing to install and nothing to sign up for. After one visit it works offline, and it can be added to the home screen of a phone or tablet.

Everything is kept on that device only. Nothing is uploaded and there is no account. Clearing the browser's data for the site clears it too.

One honest note: the studio has a guide for grown-ups on making a character from a photo using Google Gemini. If you use Gemini, the photo goes to Google. Nothing you add to the studio itself leaves the device.

The [studio page](/studio/) has pictures of every part, and the [Jazz's Studio docs](/docs/jazz-studio/) go through printing, characters and where things are kept. If you want the studio inside Sukhi Play, it is on the [download page](/download/).

**What age is Jazz's Studio for?** About seven and up. It comes in Sukhi Play switched off, so a younger child's screen stays exactly as it was until a parent adds it.

**Can my child use Jazz's Studio on an iPad?** Yes. Open sukhiplay.com/playground/studio/ in Safari. It prints one A4 page, and Add to Home Screen keeps it there, working without internet after the first visit.

**Is anything my child makes uploaded?** No. Prints, photos and doodles are kept on that device only, and there is no account to make.

## Why Sukhi Play moved from MIT to a personal-use licence

https://sukhiplay.com/blog/new-licence/ (Announcements, 2026-09-23, by Mandeep Singh)

> From 2.1, Sukhi Play is free for families to use, change and share, but never for commercial use or organisations. 2.0.2 and earlier stay under MIT.

From version 2.1, Sukhi Play and Sukhi Colouring are released under the Sukhi Play Personal Use Licence instead of MIT. They are free for individuals and families to use, change and share, and never for commercial use or for any organisation, schools and nurseries included. Everything up to and including 2.0.2 was released under MIT and stays under it.

## What changes for a family using it at home?

Nothing. Sukhi Play is still free, with no account and no paid version. You can set it up for your own children, change it to suit your family, study how it works, and give copies to other families, as long as you do not charge for them.

The code is all still public. Every line, including the parts that decide what your child can reach, is there to read.

## What is no longer allowed?

Under the new terms, none of these is permitted, whether or not anyone pays:

- **Anything commercial.** Selling it, charging for access to it, showing adverts in or around it, collecting data through it, or using it in, with or to promote a product or service.
